extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, novelists, and critics/students of narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and managing narrative method in novels: scenic vs panoramic treatment, centre of vision, authorial voice, scene placement, and the balance between subjective and objective presentation. Uses Madame Bovary as a working example to illustrate how to prepare scenes, shift perspective, and maintain tonal consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic and panoramic presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between a 'scenic' presentation (concerned with a single, particular hour and the immediate impression it produces) and a 'panoramic' or general view that surveys the story from a height.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use scenic treatment to drop the reader into an hour or moment that starts an interest or serves as a climax; use panoramic/summary to carry the story on between scenes. A novelist may mix both methods on the same page or sentence, but should manage the alternation deliberately. The scenic is best when you want the reader to watch the surge of a character's emotion; the panoramic when you need broader development or summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial voice vs 'impersonality'
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'impersonal' author keeps in the background and suppresses direct comment, yet still conveys opinions through selection and treatment of material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not confuse lack of explicit authorial comment with absence of judgement. Even when not announcing opinions in words, a writer shows what he thinks through touches on the subject, choice of details, tone, and irony. Decide how visibly the author will 'stand outside' the action and let the manner of presentation imply valuation rather than stating it bluntly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using character perspective versus author perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: The author sometimes speaks in his own voice and sometimes talks through a character's eyes and standards; both reproduce something in the author's mind but give different colours to the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose when to render a landscape, incident, or character through the author's standards and when to filter it through a character's perception (e.g., Emma's view). Be conscious of the difference: character-filtered views impart the scene with that character's mood and limits; authorial views supply wider irony or context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial (scenic) versus dramatic rendering
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictorial/scenic rendering bathes the scene in a character's mood and is not the same as dramatic staging; dramatic rendering foregrounds visible and audible facts and could be staged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the effect depends on the climate of a character's emotion, favour pictorial treatment; if the force depends on seeing and hearing events directly (bustle, speeches, jostle), favour dramatic rendering. Recognize that some scenes (e.g., a ball described through a heroine's mood) lose effect if transferred to the stage, whereas others (e.g., the cattle-show with crowd and rhetoric) survive theatrical realization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of method / adherence to a plan
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist must follow the principle he has adopted and allow himself no more latitude than required; critics look for the principle on which methods are mingled and varied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide on a guiding plan for the book and be consistent about applying it; mixed methods are permissible but should serve the subject's needs, not writerly laziness. Avoid gratuitous variation that undermines unity or confuses the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate alternation and management of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a novelist may draw on many resources (dramatic, pictorial, panoramic), he should manage how these are alternated and blended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan how scene yields to summary and summary prepares for scene. Watch how shifts in scale and method (scenic to panoramic) are handled so that each transition prepares and justifies the next moment of focus. The 'layers and stratifications' of methods should be intelligible and responsive to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place scenes where everything is ready (preparedness of occasion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene must be placed at the point where everything is ready for it—where it will illuminate a new face of the subject and advance action by a definite stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid scenes that do nothing or are insufficiently prepared; a scene that 'for lack of preparation fails to make its effect' is a weakness. Use summary or chronicle to prepare the reader so that when the scene arrives, the action is ripe and the place resonant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of the scene as structural device
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene 'holds the place of honour' as the readiest means of starting interest and raising questions, and it recurs for climaxes and resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distribute and render scenes so each contributes increasingly on rereading; let scenes articulate the book's structure (open questions, establish aspects of the story, and lead to the next stage). Use quicker summary between scenes to carry the story to subsequent climaxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing the centre of vision / focal consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine with which character (if any) the writer is to identify and from whose mind the action will be revealed; this is the 'centre of vision.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the whole subject can be rendered from one figure's point of view or whether shifts are necessary. Where the action's middle lies (e.g., Emma in Madame Bovary), make that the main focal point, but be ready to use other centres sparingly when they serve the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid haphazard or unnecessary plunges into interiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Haphazard and unnecessary plunges into the inner life of characters confuse the effect by changing focus without compensating gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift interior perspectives only when the subject demands it; avoid gratuitous 'going behind' a character that interrupts the narrative flow or muddies the reader's sense of whose story is being told.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the subject type (portrait, drama, or pictorial) before choosing method
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the novel's true subject is a portrait of character, a drama of opposing wills, or a pictorial study, because each demands different treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject is chiefly a portrait, select incidents and setting that illuminate the person and treat the world as invented to serve that portrait. If dramatic, emphasize conflict and consequential events. If pictorial, focus on rendering the life and environment vividly; choose the method that reveals the irreducible idea that the book is about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render setting as fully as characters
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject depends on the interaction between character and environment, the setting must be distinct, individual, and treated with as much salience as the protagonist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the town/place and its people integral to the picture, not mere background. If the environment is essential to the subject (as Yonville is to Emma), brood over its details until it tells alongside the central figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author must supply perception when character's intelligence is inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: If a character's perception is too limited to reveal the world properly, the author's wit must supply what is wanting; otherwise the picture will be thin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be ready to step beyond a character's consciousness to furnish necessary context, but mask this intervention artfully so the reader is not jarred by an abrupt change of mind. Provide other standpoints or an authorial view to complete the portrait without destroying immersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disguise perspective transitions to avoid dislocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitions from a character's subjective viewpoint to the author's external vantage must be made without awkwardness or sudden exposure of the author changing his part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid blunt 'going behind' comments or visible shifts that shout the author's intrusion. Use subtlety, tonal continuity, and structural preparation to make changes of perspective feel natural and integral to the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the character at a certain distance to prevent over-identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain an air of aloofness, even when entering a character's mind, so the reader does not become wholly immersed and then jolted when the author resumes an external stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a 'hint of irony' or tonal distance while rendering subjectivity so that the author's later supersession of the character's view feels natural. This preserves both the immediacy of subjective moments and the author's freedom to judge or broaden the perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use irony discreetly as a tool to balance valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Irony prevents the reader from being entirely lost in a character's consciousness and allows the author to imply valuation without blunt assertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imply the author's judgement through tone rather than explicit statements; the close-at-hand irony should be enough to prevent full identification and to permit the author to create wider contexts (other characters, settings) beyond the character's grasp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare other characters' perspectives when required for the ending
rubrics_metrics.description: If the climax or resolution depends on another character's later reaction or discovery, that character's inner life must be prepared earlier in the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant episodes, history, or glimpses into secondary characters (e.g., Charles's youth and life) so they exist 'in reserve' for the climax. Early preparation makes the final stroke—such as a revealing discovery—instantly felt and plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overt authorial boasting or malicious intrusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Open maltreatment of one's own story—boasting of independence or explicit authorial meddling—can disconcert the reader and damage the narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from breaking the narrative to proclaim the author's freedom to contradict or mock characters. Maintain the illusion of the story's coherence; let any authorial judgement be exercised with restraint and craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy in variation: allow no more latitude than required
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist should not take more liberty with method than the subject needs; variation should be economical and purposeful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only introduce a new method or perspective when it advances the subject. Excessive variety for its own sake weakens unity; measured use of resources keeps the work 'well-made' and effective.
